title: Machine Learning: a model is only good if it beats a simple guess
intro: ML work is mostly careful evaluation. You build a baseline, split data honestly, compare models, and record every experiment so results are reproducible.
outcome: A logged experiment showing a model versus its baseline on held-out data, with a clear ship / don't-ship decision.

steps.title: Learn how AI, ML and deep learning fit together
steps.what: Know the vocabulary and run each idea on a tiny example.
how: Open AI fundamentals on this page and read the hierarchy.
Run Learn rules from data, then compare the learned rules with the hand-written rule.
Train the XOR network with and without a hidden layer.
Enter a confusion matrix and read why accuracy alone misleads.
steps.done_when: You can say why a model needs a baseline and a test set.
mistakes: Treating accuracy as the whole story on unbalanced classes.
Calling every model 'AI' without saying what kind.
steps.ask: Explain supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning with an example from my work.

steps.title: Define the target and the metric
steps.what: What exactly will the model predict, and how will you score it?
how: Pick the target (e.g. daily revenue or cost).
Pick an error metric the business understands (MAE in dollars).
Decide what 'good enough' means.
steps.done_when: Target, metric and the pass mark are written down.
mistakes: Optimising a metric nobody cares about.
steps.ask: Help me choose a target and metric for my data.

steps.title: Check you have enough data
how: See the readiness strip: 100+ records and 20+ distinct days.
If short, import more data on My data first.
mistakes: Training on a handful of rows.
steps.ask: Is my dataset big enough to train a model?

steps.title: Build the baseline first
steps.what: The simplest possible guess (e.g. the average) is the bar to beat.
how: Open the ML Lab: every run reports a baseline score next to the model score.
If the model barely beats the baseline, it isn't worth the complexity.
mistakes: Skipping the baseline.
Comparing a model to nothing.
steps.ask: Why does a baseline matter and what is mine?

steps.title: Split by time, not randomly
steps.what: Training on the future and testing on the past is leakage.
how: The lab splits chronologically: earlier days train, later days test.
Never let the test set influence choices.
steps.done_when: You can explain why the split is by time.
mistakes: Random splits on time series.
Tuning on the test set.
steps.ask: Explain data leakage using my dataset.

steps.title: Choose features
steps.what: Inputs the model can use at prediction time.
how: Pick the features offered in the ML Lab.
Ask: would I know this value when I need the prediction?
Start small.
steps.done_when: Every feature is available at prediction time.
mistakes: Using the target (or a copy) as a feature.
steps.ask: Which features are safe to use and which leak?

steps.title: Train and compare
how: Train each model in the ML Lab.
Compare test score versus baseline and train versus test.
A big gap between train and test means overfitting.
steps.done_when: At least 2 models compared on the same split.
mistakes: Picking by train score.
steps.ask: Compare my model runs and say which to prefer.

steps.title: Log and review experiments
steps.what: If it isn't recorded, it didn't happen.
how: Every run is stored in the experiment log.
Note what you changed between runs.
steps.done_when: The log shows what you tried and why.
mistakes: Changing three things at once.

steps.title: Decide: ship or not
how: Does it beat the baseline by more than noise?
What happens when it's wrong?
How will you notice drift?
Note: models in this lab are for learning; they aren't deployed anywhere.
steps.done_when: You wrote ship / don't ship and the reason.
mistakes: Shipping without a monitoring plan.
steps.ask: Help me write the ship or don't-ship decision.

steps.title: Follow the learning path and prove each module
steps.what: Seven levels from foundations to MLOps, each ending in a gate project.
how: Open the Machine learning learning path above.
Read the 'Built here / Partly here / Study outside / Can't run here' badge on each module before you start it.
Do the 'Prove it' task, then tick the module only when you could explain it to someone else.
Mark a level's gate passed only after you have shipped its project.
steps.done_when: At least one level has every module ticked and its gate marked.
mistakes: Ticking a module after reading about it but never building anything.
Skipping Level 1: honest validation is the whole job.
steps.ask: Where am I on the ML path and what should I do next?

steps.title: See overfitting happen
steps.what: Training error always falls as a model gets more flexible; only held-out error shows the truth.
how: Open ML tools > Bias and variance and run it.
Find the best degree, then change the seed and run again.
Say which rows are underfit and which are overfit, and why.
steps.done_when: You can explain why the best degree moves a little when the seed changes.
mistakes: Trusting one random split of a small data set.
steps.ask: Explain the train versus validation error table in plain words.

steps.title: Write the algorithms once, by hand
steps.what: Gradient descent, kNN, a tree and naive Bayes teach what each model assumes.
how: Open ML tools > Gradient descent and make it diverge, crawl, then converge.
Open Algorithms from scratch and raise the tree depth from 1 to 10.
Compare every model with the baseline accuracy.
steps.done_when: You know which model wins on the moons data and why a straight line cannot.
mistakes: Reading results without comparing to the baseline.
steps.ask: Why does logistic regression struggle on this data?

steps.title: Pick the threshold with money, not 0.5
steps.what: ROC-AUC ranks; the cut-off is a business choice.
how: Open ML tools > Scores and thresholds and load the sample.
Make a miss cost 10 times a false alarm and see the best threshold move.
Compare with the cost of never raising an alarm.
steps.done_when: You can state the best threshold and its cost for your own costs.
mistakes: Defaulting to 0.5.
Judging a rare-event model by accuracy.
steps.ask: Help me set a threshold if a miss costs 10 times a false alarm.

steps.title: Scan for leakage before you trust a score
steps.what: A leak is a column you would not have at prediction time.
how: Open ML tools > Leakage scan and load the sample.
Read each flag: near-perfect single-feature signal, outcome-sounding names, ID columns, duplicates.
Remove the flagged columns in ML Lab and watch the score drop to something believable.
steps.done_when: The flagged columns are removed or justified in writing.
mistakes: Celebrating a score above 0.95 without asking why.
steps.ask: Which of my columns might leak the target?

steps.title: Check drift and read an automatic search honestly
steps.what: Models go stale in three ways: the inputs change (input drift), the mix of outcomes changes (label drift), or accuracy falls (performance drift). Practice all three with PSI, a KS test and a confidence interval. Then run an automatic feature and model search and learn what it can and cannot tell you.
how: Open ML > Build and check ML pieces > Input and label drift, click Load sample and run it. Read PSI and the KS p-value. Which bin moved most?
Switch to labels and compare two sets of class labels. Why can this matter when the inputs look unchanged?
Open Performance drift, load the sample and find the first period flagged as a real drop. Why is a small dip in the first months not flagged?
Open Automatic search, load the sample, and run it. Which column was ignored and why? Read the warnings.
Add a column that copies the target and rerun. What does the tool say about the score?
steps.done_when: You can say which kind of drift you are looking at, and why an automatic search's winning score is a little optimistic.
mistakes: Retraining automatically every time PSI crosses 0.1.
Trusting accuracy from a tiny period without its interval.
Letting automatic search use a row ID or the answer as a feature.
Using the same data to pick features and report the final score.
steps.ask: PSI is 0.3 on a feature the model barely uses. Should we retrain?

steps.title: Train a network, check its gradients, and look inside text models
steps.what: Train a small neural network written in numpy and watch it learn xor, which a straight line cannot. Prove the backward pass is right with a gradient check. Then see attention weights, how a tokenizer builds its vocabulary by merging pairs, and how a concept-based search finds documents that share no words with the query.
how: Open Neural network, train on xor with hidden layers 8. Then train with no hidden layer. What changes and why?
Click Check the gradients. Explain in one line why the two columns agree.
Raise the learning rate to 3. What happens to the loss?
Open Attention and run it with and without the causal mask. Which words can the first word see?
Open Tokenizer (BPE), load the sample and run it. Which pair was merged first and why?
Open Meaning search (LSA), load the sample and find the document with a keyword score of 0 but a high concept score.
steps.done_when: You can explain why xor needs a hidden layer, what a gradient check proves, and why a token is not always a word.
mistakes: Calling attention weights an explanation of what a trained model 'thinks'.
Training until training accuracy is perfect and ignoring the test points.
Assuming one word is one token when estimating cost.
Treating the random attention demo as meaningful.
steps.ask: Why does a network with no hidden layer fail on xor?
